title: Continue, break off or repeat: the decision after the attack starts
outcomes: Decides to continue, break off or accept a repetition by checking whether the forcing line still ends in mate or material
Recognises that a missing piece makes the same sacrifice fail
Accepts a forced repetition when every other move loses material
Treats "never break off" as a rule of thumb, not a law

steps.text: In **Before you sacrifice, count every piece that must arrive** you decided whether to start. Once the attack is on, the question returns every move: **continue**, **break off** or **accept a repetition**? Continue while the forcing line still ends in mate or material and every piece has arrived. Break off when a needed piece cannot come. Repeat when a draw is the best you can force. 'Never break off' is a **rule of thumb**.

steps.caption: White is in trouble. Look at what the checks achieve.

line.say: Qxh6+ is check, and the engine rates it best.

claims.statement: Qxh6+ is the engine's best move (depth 16).
Qxe5 is at least 4 pawns worse than Qxh6+ (depth 16).
The engine rates the position as level (depth 16).

steps.text: A repetition is not a failure of nerve; it is a result. In the board position the checks keep the game level, while the natural-looking Qxe5 loses at least four pawns. Ask three things: does the forcing line still end in mate or material? has every piece arrived? what is the best I can force if one has not? The simple winning move, if you have one, is often better than a long attack: also a **rule of thumb**.

steps.prompt: White considers Rxg6+. Predict for each: continue, break off or accept a repetition? Then check.
In your next game with an attack on, stop after each forcing move and write: continue, break off or repeat. Which of the three do you expect to choose least often?
